messages.author: 06199470668a2843
messages.subject: Does Distance underestimate transect area?
parts:
Hi all,

I am using distance sampling to monitor bird densities on farmland. I've
come upon a confusing issue related to the method program Distance uses t=
o
calculate transect area.

By my understanding, the area of a given transect is calculated as [2 *
transect length * transect half-width] - where half-width is truncation
distance or effective strip width, as necessary for the specific use. Thi=
s
supposes a square transect shape. The resulting area is then used in the
calculation of a density estimate.

Plotting the transects I walked on a GIS system, it occurred to me that
the actual area surveyed is not of that shape, though. Rather, there is a
hemispherical "cap" of radius [transect half-width] at each end of the
transect, unless the observer ignores sightings behind him when starting
out and culls sightings that were beyond the transect end-point after
stopping. So the actual area that the detections are gathered from would
be [(2 * transect length * transect half-width) + (pi * transect
half-width^2)].

Assuming, as in my case, a transect length of 500m and and an average ESW
of ~50m, this makes for a ~15% underestimation of transect area and thus
an overestimation of density by the same amount. It would also bias the
result of, e.g., using projected transect area on a GIS system to estimat=
e
the percentage of vegetation in a transect.

Am I misinterpreting something here? Would the expected "behaviour" of th=
e
observer consist of excluding these two add-on hemispheres from the
surveyed area, thus conforming to the square shape? I definitely did not
do that - in that case, should I adjust the density estimates given by
Distance by the necessary percentage?

best regards
florian


--=20

messages.author: 6e15de0134e98c08
messages.subject: Re: Does Distance underestimate transect area?
parts:
Hi Florian, list,

Strictly speaking, when you are doing a line transect you must ignore=20
all observations "outside" the rectangle that you refer to, defined by=20
the transect.

And note that the problem is not just about the way the transect area is=20
calculated, but also a more subtle yet equally important one. If you=20
consider data from the "hemispherical cap" you refer to, an half circle=20
at each end of the transects, then you are mixing data from line=20
transects and point transects - your transect becomes in fact a line=20
transect + a point transect (1 half of a point transect at each end).=20
The analysis of such data is not possible using conventional methods,=20
because now you do not know what is the underlying distribution of=20
distances is (which is assumed uniform for lines and triangular for=20
points in the conventional setting, which is typically guaranteed by=20
placing many samplers - lines or points - using a random design=20
independent of animal distribution).

So, in short, you need to ignore the data "outside" the rectangular=20
transect. In most situations, with large areas, this is not an issue and=20
simple to do. A more complicated approach, if your half circles are so=20
large that a good proportion of the data comes from them, is to change=20
your design to points rather than lines, or (which for simplicity I=20
would try to avoid) to do both but then extra care must be used to=20
ensure independence of the two source of data, which would be analyzed=20
separately.

Cheers

Tiago
